note: Top 500 videos by sales + views (of 2063 studied). Refreshed with every publish.

tier_defs.1: Videos selling our exact products — magnesium complex and cortisol support for women. Copy the recipe closely.
tier_defs.2: Calming drinks and de-stress supplements chasing the same benefits — cortisol, sleep, bloat — just not ours. Keep the hook, swap in our product.
tier_defs.3: Completely different product worlds — the formats are the loot. Steal the format, never the topic.

tier_intro.1: These videos sell our exact product. Copy the recipe closely.
tier_intro.2: Supplements chasing the same benefits — hair growth, skin, wellness. Keep the hook structure, adapt the words to our product.
tier_intro.3: Completely different product worlds. Steal the format, never the topic.

1.name: 'You're not fat, that's high cortisol' body-part pointing symptom checklist
1.hook: Creator direct to camera — car seat, bedroom, gym — index finger up, running down body parts with a matching illustration popping into the corner for each: 'if your pooch looks like this, or your chin looks like this, or your hips look like this, you're probably not even fat, it's just high cortisol' (np.deals, hey.itspaige, pao.stephanii, resetwithmaddi, wellnessbeautynurse77). The single biggest earner in the angle is the silent version — three pairs of hands pinching sagging skin at the chin, jaw and underarm under 'lo que odias mas de tu cara' ($42.2k, 898/day, no talking at all) — and the next-strongest variation opens on borrowed authority: 'did you see that nurse who went viral saying if your chin looks like this, your pooch like that, you're not fat, you just have high cortisol' ($17.6k at 1,259/day). A caption-only cut also wins big: creator quietly opening the bottle while a long text block reads 'I wish more women knew that losing your sex drive, gaining in your belly and face, hair thinning & loss, rage, irritability, anxiety, fatigue, waking up at 2am and insomnia are all signs your body is stuck in fight or flight' ($6.7k at 250/day). Keep the whole stack the winners stack: lower pooch, double chin, hips/armpits, back rolls, puffy face, thinning hair, night cramps, 2-3am waking, sugar cravings, rage/irritability, no sex drive, brain fog, fatigue.
1.why: It renames a body the viewer already hates as a hormone problem rather than a discipline problem — that reframe removes shame and creates instant identification — and pointing at one body part at a time with an illustration keeps the viewer scanning herself for the next hit instead of scrolling.

1.name: Doctor/nurse exam-room symptom skit ('all right, what's wrong with you?')
1.hook: Two-role skit shot by one creator: she snaps on a hot-pink exam glove or picks up a clipboard, asks 'all right, what's wrong with you?', and cuts to herself as the patient — 'I can't stop eating sugar' — then the nurse guesses the rest: 'and let me guess, your hair is thinning and you've got a lower pooch that won't go away?', with a thinning-hairline photo and a belly-pooch inset dropping in as she says each one (elainevdvwidrick $37.3k at 2,485/day and $27.1k at 1,354/day; social.nurse.stephanie, holisticglpgirly's GLP-1 side-effects version at $23.4k / 2,604/day). It resolves on a handwritten 'HIGH CORTISOL' clipboard reveal, then the label and the cost-vs-buying-separately math. The second-strongest variation is the Spanish comedy POV skit — 'how the hell did you get so jacked?' at the kitchen counter, or the water-retention/mother-in-law bit — same two-character structure, comedy instead of clinic (tumejorsaluddiaria, shopwithrenri, momoishopy).
1.why: Having the symptom read back to you by a 'clinician' who already knows the answer converts a scroll into a diagnosis, and the patient character does the objection-raising so the sell never sounds like an ad; the skit format also buys 40-70 seconds of watch time before the product ever appears.

1.name: Before/after de-bloat + weight-drop reveal ('before taking magnesium - 188 lbs')
1.hook: A single unglamorous 'before' still or clip held for 2-3 seconds with a blunt caption stamped on it — 'before taking magnesium + 188lbs', 'yo sin saber como desinflarme + 181lb', 'me retaining water because of stress + 216lbs' — over a trending sound, then the after slide (ketryn.lawrence runs this on repeat at 354/day, 303/day, 188/day; melanniebrownn, livedstories, avalawrence_, charashop; several are 3-slide photo carousels). The next-strongest variation is spoken: creator turns in a gym set and says 'this is what a high cortisol body looks like' before cutting to the slimmer after ($10.8k), and a third runs the face — 'proof cortisol face is real (4wks ago)' / 'your sign to lower cortisol (1 month ago)' — a puffy, tired, breakout-prone open cutting to a sharper jaw and clear skin (victoria.wellnesss $9.1k, andresdoesitbetter, cliplagoon, babyglowup1, luna350782). Bottle appears at ~6s in the final slide with the 8-forms label readable.
1.why: The 'before' frame is deliberately worse-looking than anything a normal ad would show, which reads as real and stops the scroll on self-recognition; the number or the timestamp does the persuading, so the video needs no script, no credential and almost no production.

1.name: Reply-to-comment testimonial ('mamita, I told you what it did for me')
1.hook: Creator answers a pinned buyer comment on camera, bottle already in hand at 0-5s, talking straight into the lens like she's continuing a conversation: 'y es que mamita, no solo a vos, sino a 1.5 millones mas de personas que lo han comprado aqui en el tiki-tiki' over a comment reading 'yo lo tome y me ayudo mucho' (tuchera_lasalvi owns this format — $18.3k at 469/day, $15.9k at 886/day, $4k at 396/day, and eight more). The next-strongest variation is the un-prompted personal testimonial with the same intimacy: 'me because I'm 34 and that girl said this 8-in-1 magnesium made her stop waking up at 3am, killed her sugar cravings and her cortisol finally chilled out — I could kiss her rn' as a caption while she opens the bottle and swallows a capsule on camera (farmerkay22), and the excited new-product reveal from a holistic creator ('I've had two weeks on it and this is going to change the game', mayaholistic1 $13.7k / $13.6k). Benefits the winners stack: de-bloating a dress size, regular bathroom trips, sleeping through without dreaming, less stress, muscle and joint pain, dosing guidance (two capsules, 5-6pm or before bed).
1.why: A reply to a real comment is social proof the viewer can verify by reading the thread, and answering an objection ('does it hurt your stomach?', 'how do I take it?') moves a warm buyer over the line without a single ad-sounding line; it is also the cheapest content in the set — no props, no set, no script.

1.name: Objection-handler myth-buster (spot-the-fake, wrong timing, the diarrhea question)
1.hook: Creator in the car, finger up, opening on a hard negative: 'falso, falso, falso y falso — y si amigo, el mio es el original, y te voy a ensenar en menos de 30 segundos por que no quiero que caigas en la estafa', over a grid of TikTok Shop listings of the same bottle at wildly different prices, resolving on the official verified shop badge circled in red (trendtoksetter31, $27.8k at 397/day plus a $2.5k follow-up). Two other variations carry the angle: the how-to-take correction from a clinician — 'they shove magnesium down your throat and say it'll fix your cortisol, but nobody told you how to take it' / 'a que hora se debe tomar el magnesio? porque la mayoria lo esta tomando mal' (faithfuldoc $17k at 678/day, lilia_latinacreator $17.8k at 379/day, social.nurse.stephanie, marketerohispano) — and the side-effect reassurance reply: 'it gives you a lot of diarrhea — relax, it happened to me too and I stopped taking it for a few days because I got scared, then I learned this is super common' ($13.3k at 402/day). Also proven: 'don't buy this stuff anymore' with five competitor bottles tossed aside, and the 'cortisol face isn't a thing' rebuttal.
1.why: Every one of these opens on a doubt the buyer already has — is mine fake, am I wasting it, why does it wreck my stomach, does this even work — so it captures high-intent viewers at the exact moment they would have abandoned the purchase, and answering the objection publicly converts the whole comment section, not just the asker.

1.name: Head-to-head 'which magnesium is better' comparison + supplement-stack replacement
1.hook: Creator holds up the pile they are about to replace and refuses it on camera: 'look, I don't care if you guys like [brand] — there is no way you can convince me to take this, with this, with this, with this, with this', five separate bottles going down one by one before the single bottle comes up (joshuazitting $14k at 292/day, thatrendy $6.8k at 219/day, autumatic4thepeople). The next-strongest variation is the credentialed head-to-head: a pharmacist or researcher holding two bottles side by side — 'which is better? let's compare so you can make the best decision' — cutting between both Supplement Facts panels with a finger on the oxide line and a running check/X caption (rphreviews $12.4k at 311/day, drew.review, healthandbeautyrn), and the prescription-vs-natural version, 'Xanax versus natural anxiety reducers, which is better from a doctor's perspective' ($7k at 334/day).
1.why: It arrives at the exact moment of choice — the viewer is already shopping magnesium and wants permission to pick one — and reading the label on camera makes the decision feel like the viewer's own research rather than a pitch; the stack-replacement version adds cost math the buyer can check.

1.name: Celebrity / influencer magnesium stitch
1.hook: Stitch of a known pair caught on camera in a van casually talking about the product between takes — 'yeah, you took it? yeah, it calms you down' — with a persistent caption naming them and framing it as an overheard endorsement rather than an ad; no product shot at all, the whole video is the borrowed moment plus the caption redirect (tea.daily_, $3.3k on 1M views, 60/day over 55 days).
1.why: A famous person saying it works in an unguarded moment reads as proof the brand couldn't buy, and the stitch lets the creator ride an already-viral clip's reach; the cost is that it converts poorly per view (lowest GPM in the set) because nothing is ever demonstrated or explained.

2.name: Before/after transformation testimonial ("I was 198lbs / start of summer: bloated, insecure")
2.hook: Opens on the unflattering 'before' with a caption naming the shame, then cuts to the after. Top earner: woman in a hot tub, caption "POV you got tired of being the bigback of the friend group", cutting to a slim beach reveal (7657796013033393421, $786/day). Next-strongest variations, both very high velocity: the timestamped caption stack — "Start of 2026: losing confidence / big back / bloated" over a full-body mirror selfie (7659534559318461710) — and the weight-number version, "208lbs — I was the ugliest outta my friends" over a poolside group photo (7649604835188296991). Several members are photo carousels; the credentialed 'this turns into this when your gut is clogged' overlay variant sits inside this angle too.
2.why: It sells the outcome as already achieved by someone the viewer recognises as their own starting point, and the caption does the emotional work in under 3 seconds so the proof shot lands before the scroll.

2.name: Direct-to-camera holy-grail discovery testimonial + ingredient breakdown
2.hook: Creator bursts in mid-reaction, as if they just found out: "How have I been sleeping on this for this long?" while lifting a crop top and gesturing, caption "YOU'RE SEEING THIS JUST IN TIME FOR SUMMER" — then hard-cuts into ingredient benefit cards (7647060239807679758, $16.9k, the single highest-GMV winner in the set, and repeated by the same creator at 7656381689731550477 / 7663046432370314526 / 7661950028449107230). Next-strongest variation is the calmer skeptic-turned-believer read — "I thought it was a scam, but…" / "I fear this stuff actually does work" — same structure, lower volume. Nearly every member pairs the reaction with a named-ingredient explainer (what it is → what it does for you).
2.why: Discovery energy plus scarcity ("just in time") makes the viewer feel late rather than sold to, and the ingredient cards convert that urgency into a rational reason to buy before the video ends.

2.name: Symptom-checklist body-flaw callout — "how to come back unrecognizable / mog your friends"
2.hook: Creator faces camera and immediately reads out a list of visible body flaws over matching overlays: "How to come back to school a different person — if you hate taking your shirt off at the pool, you have pity titties or you have the gobbler, you need this", caption "how to mog the school", with inset photos of an overweight man in a pool and a round belly (7654367673760927006, top GMV). The next-strongest variation is the numbered-list read — "How to become unrecognizable in 60 days: 1. Get rid of the bloat (you're not fat)" with problem-proof close-ups of belly pinch, jaw, sock-marked ankles (7659116858699730190) — and the Spanish "3 maneras de desincharte este verano" version. Each symptom gets its own overlay beat, then the product lands as the single fix.
2.why: The hook is a diagnostic, not a pitch: the viewer self-identifies on symptom 1 or 2 and has to stay for the fix, and the overlays do the shaming so the creator can stay likeable. The numbered structure also promises a finite, watchable video.

2.name: Skit / scenario sketch — the relatable symptom played out as a scene
2.hook: Cold-opens mid-scene with no setup. Top earner: a two-role doctor's-office sketch — patient storms in holding up stained underwear, "So what brings you in today?" "So why do my mom's panties look like this?" (7648070807415049502, $4.5k), with the symptom list delivered as dialogue and notebook illustrations. Next-strongest: the gynecologist exam sketch (7644775616453020959) and the POV relationship scenes — "POV: you're 47, divorce and cortisol hit you like a brick wall" (7662117014240070925, $303/day) and the boyfriend-breakup POV. The product arrives late, as the scene's punchline resolution.
2.why: Comedy buys permission to name embarrassing symptoms out loud, and the scene format keeps retention long enough to reach a 30-60s product reveal that a straight ad could never hold.

2.name: Counterfeit / real-vs-fake myth-buster ("this is fake, this is fake — you got scammed")
2.hook: Creator holds up two near-identical tubs, one in each hand: "Y'all, I am so sick of doing this — but this is fake and this is fake", caption "This is a SCAM…" (7662485182531800333, $457/day on 6 days live — the fastest earner in the angle). Next-strongest variation is the casual kitchen version: creator slicing fruit, "I hate to break it to you, but if this didn't work for you, you probably got scammed", caption "Why are U falling for SCAMZ in 2026…" (7639556966292966669), followed by side-by-side listing screenshots, verified-seller badge, and 5-star review counts. A credentialed variant exists (nutrition coach, "Don't get scammed").
2.why: It hijacks a buying objection the viewer already has (does this stuff even work?) and converts it into a reason the product IS real — the 'scam' is the other listing, not the category. Highest mean revenue percentile of any device in the set.

2.name: Celebrity / influencer stitch — borrowed podcast moment redirected to the product
2.hook: Stitches a celebrity clip and answers it. Top earner: Kylie on a podcast — "What were you craving? Everything. I ate a pint of ice cream every night" — with the caption "who's gonna tell Kylie this exists", then the creator cuts to themselves making the drink (7649888535528377614, $5,992). The same borrowed clip was re-run by several creators with different captions ("How does Kylie not know it exists", "Even Kylie Jenner likes this stuff too?"). Next-strongest variations: the comment-section reveal — "They got Huda taking this too" with the comment circled in red (7651743222296825119) — and the borrowed-movie-clip physique open ("pov us mogging all summer").
2.why: The celebrity supplies the attention and the implied endorsement; the creator only has to supply the redirect. Borrowed credibility with zero production cost.

2.name: Cortisol reframe — "signs I didn't realize were high cortisol" symptom checklist / myth-buster
2.hook: Caption-led reframe over a mundane shot: "Cortisol doesn't really affect ur body that much… / Oh… really??" over a relaxed restaurant table (7657365600754339103, top GMV and the highest velocity in the angle). Next-strongest: the walk-through-the-kitchen open captioned "Signs I didn't realize were high cortisol" (7652512155362790669) with a green-check ingredient list (ashwagandha, magnesium glycinate, L-theanine, vitamin D), and the blunt myth-bust "You're not old and ugly, you just have high cortisol" (7647324941469142286) with skin/hair symptom close-ups. Symptoms named: puffy face, wired-but-tired, exhausted all day then awake at night, sugar cravings, snapping at your husband over nothing.
2.why: It renames a pile of symptoms the viewer already has as one fixable cause, which converts vague self-criticism into a product-shaped problem — and the cortisol frame is the closest thing in this whole competitor set to what we actually sell.
